title: Four months ago, I started experimenting with AI
author: Hamsterboyi
selftext:
Four months ago, I started experimenting with AI and a simple idea.

I've always loved roguelikes and card games, and I wanted to see if I could create something that my friends and I would actually enjoy playing together.

At the time, I wasn't planning to develop a game.

I wasn't starting a business.

I wasn't even looking for a long-term project.

It was just a fun experiment that started with a single prompt.

I also have a full-time job completely unrelated to game development, so most of the work happened during evenings, weekends, and whenever I found a bit of free time.

Using tools like Claude, Astra, and Higgsfield, I kept experimenting with mechanics, cards, events, and new ideas. Whenever something felt fun, I kept it. Whenever something didn't, I changed it.

The biggest surprise wasn't the AI itself.

It was how much I enjoyed the process.

What started as a small experiment slowly grew into The Unwritten by Yoji, and four months later I've just released Version 9.4.

More than anything, this project has simply been a fun creative journey and an opportunity to build the kind of game that I personally enjoy playing.

If you'd like to take a look, you're more than welcome. And if you decide to play it, I'd genuinely love to hear your honest feedback, good or bad.

Game Page: https://adarbogos.itch.io/the-unwritten

comments.author: HitMePat
comments.body: I made it as far as the first screen with How To Play....how many games have you seen OP where the first screen the player sees hits them with a wall of text that takes 5+ minutes to read?  That's going to turn off most players immediately.  I recommend you figure out a way to introduce all those concepts piece by piece in small bites as they become relevant in the game.  Let the players actually experience something that is actual game play in the first minute, not reading a dissertation.

comments.author: Hamsterboyi
comments.body: Thanks for giving the game a chance, and I hear you, fair point. The plan is to move the How To Play info into small popups that show up while you're actually playing, right when each concept becomes relevant. Believe it or not, it started as just a few lines, and over time it grew into that wall of text. I'm planning to add the in-game popups in 9.5 :)

comments.author: Head-Cucumber-7222
comments.body:
I played a bit and here is my stream of consciousness thoughts:

If you're going to make slay the spire (StS), just make it. I disliked the 3 card shuffle after battles, as a strategist type game i want to craft my deck, not play dollar-street-scams where I have to pay attention to where a card is going. I dont think paying to turn over 1 card or forcing the player to pay attention are compelling gameplay elements. It feels tacked on and not in theme of the genre (StS).

I didnt read the beginning wall of text, I just jumped into gameplay. On the "Last paragraph" now, whose art is kind of clashing with its name. Hiding the monster/enemy actions feels bad as a player, as it robs me of the strategic counterplay. i Have 3 defends, poison, attack. Should I defend? Attack? I have no idea. Hiding the monster next move seems on the surface like a differentiator from StS but actually robs the player of the core gameplay expectation. I ended turn and have no idea what the monster actually did, but my health didn't go down so yay?

The text is kind of small in a lot of places and the flavor text and gameplay text kind of mix together. Dark purple thin font over black is probably failing most color contrast accessibility and it's difficult to read.

Oh, I died in part 2 salt flats. I wasn't quite sure what I was chosing in between rounds, different maps? Like, I get you're going for a reading / book theme, but in terms of gameplay it's a bit confusing. I find this often with AI writing and gameplay, the AI understands the metaphor, but it gets lost in translating to the human. When making a game we can use the fictive universe along with clear player affordances. The end screen doesn't have the "Continue" button above the fold, so I have to scroll down in-game to get to it, which is rare and could cause players to get soft-locked on this page.

Again, as a new player, what does this mean?  
The Tale Breaks Off

Your story ends between the pages. But nothing here is wasted.

"Rise," says the First Traveler, extending a gauntleted hand. "You are in excellent company."

"Every story ends unfinished. Every page strengthens the next draft."

Buttons: The Scriptorium, Soul Vessel

Wtf is the Scriptorium or Soul Vessel???? Again, I'm trying to give a new-to-your-game-but-gaming-veteran player's perspective. So you can rightly say all this is explained in the first screen. However with the TikTokification of our attention spans that excuse has left our pocket.

  
Seems like a cool game with more systems to explore. Good on you for finishing it to this level!  If I was working on this, I would do a text removal pass - all the weird little AI "asides" of flavor text next to gameplay text.

replies.author: Hamsterboyi
replies.body:
Thank you, seriously. This is exactly the kind of feedback I've been missing. I don't get much of it, and a detailed play-through from someone who knows the genre is gold.

You're right on a lot of this. The wall of text is going away in favor of short tips that pop up when each thing actually matters. The in-world names (Scriptorium, Soul Vessel) clearly need a plain explanation next to them, and the Continue button on the end screen should never need scrolling. I'm also taking another look at the hidden enemy moves, the readability of the text, and the card shuffle after fights.

All of it is going into the 0.9.5 update. Thanks again for taking the time to play it and write all this up.

comments.author: hellomyoldfrien
comments.body: Love that it started as something for you friends, those are always the ones that end up feeling the most fun to play. Curious how you kept the card art consistent across that many versions, I had to start running mine through Magnific because the style kept drifting every update.

replies.author: Hamsterboyi
replies.body:
Thank you! Yeah, it started as a little game for my friends and just kept growing from there.

Keeping the art consistent was the thing I worried about most too. What ended up working for me (everything is made in Higgsfield)

One fixed recipe for every card. A single subject, centered, floating in an empty pure black void, with a glow in the card type's color (red for attacks, cyan for defense, violet for specials, gold for utility). Since the background and the glow never change, around 190 cards still read as one set even though every subject is different.

I prompt for what the card does, not just its name. A double hit gets a doubled blade, an area attack gets several slash trails. That keeps the art readable and stops the model from drifting into its own look.

The game draws the card frame, the text and the soft edge fade in code, so the image only ever has to be "the thing in the dark".

For characters there's one canon portrait, and every new pose or redesign is an edit of that painting passed in as a reference. Text-only regenerations were exactly where my drift used to come from.

Same idea for the monsters. They all follow one written art direction (dark, gaunt, more Diablo than cute), and each one is cut out of its background, so they all stand on the game's own scenes instead of each bringing its own. When a monster gets redrawn, it's an edit of its existing painting, never a fresh prompt.

Small defects like a lit corner or a stray border get fixed afterwards with a small script instead of a re-roll, so a good composition never gets swapped for a worse one.

I haven't needed an upscaler for any of this, for me the fix was keeping the recipe identical every time. What are you working on? Would love to see it.
